item.title: Higher Prices Test Holiday Shoppers
item.description:
Holiday sales are expected to rise this season, but inflation means shoppers may be spending more without bringing home more goods, while value and convenience remain key drivers. On Bloomberg This Weekend, Bloomberg Intelligence Senior Retail Analyst Poonam Goyal tells hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini how AI is reshaping shopping and helping consumers search for products, track prices and find deals. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Chloe Chaplain, Joe Mayes and Lucy White

item.title: What Happened to JFK-Era Intel Records?
item.description:
Fifty years after John F. Kennedy's assassination, Disclosure podcast's Jason Leopold requested the US Defense Intelligence Agency's daily briefings for the surrounding two months, a potential trove of details about foreign governments' contemporary planning and reactions. Twelve years later, he received a response -- three days' worth of briefings, with redactions, 41 pages in all. Jason and co-host Matt Topic delve into the secrecy surrounding the Kennedy-era records, what has become of nearly two months' worth of briefings and what could have led to the destruction of intelligence reports from a pivotal moment in US history. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Nvidia Blackwell Chips Turn Up at China Site Tied to Alice Huang
item.description:
A pair of Chinese firms installed Nvidia Corp.’s powerful Blackwell semiconductors in a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, the woman at the heart of a controversy surrounding the US chipmaker. The gear installed at the Yangtze River Delta Project included a GB300 NVL72 rack, among Nvidia’s most powerful products, according to a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November. item.title: Isabella Weber's Vision for an Affordability Agenda
item.description:
The most important word in politics right now is affordability. It was a winning issue in the midterms for Democrats, and one of the reasons why people across Europe are out in the streets protesting: Food, housing, and energy are getting more expensive by the day. During the height of the pandemic, we talked a lot about inflation with Isabella Weber, and her on what governments can do to make life more affordable has evolved into a book called Anti-Fascist Economics: In Defense of Affordability, Dignity, and Democracy. It is part-history, part-manifesto, and it maps out why things got so expensive and what can be done to get prices down. Today, we speak to Weber about why CPI, in her opinion, is a misleading measure, why fridges got cheaper but groceries got pricier, rebuilding state capacity, strategies for price controls, China's strategic pork reserve, and her new book. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Lucy White

item.title: Marc Levinson on How UPS Created Modern Logistics
item.description:
UPS was founded nearly a century ago in the basement of a Seattle saloon by James E. Casey and his business partner Claude Ryan. It is now hard to imagine modern, globalized life, and the logistics required to prop it up, without the innovations Casey and his partners at UPS cooked up during the company's early decades. Marc Levinson has just written a biography of Casey and the company he founded — UPS Man: James E. Casey and the Creation of Modern Logistics — which was a lot harder to do than you might imagine, because Casey shunned the spotlight and his contributions were virtually unknown outside of UPS. In today's episode, Levinson tells us why UPS is so secretive about its history, how Casey and his partners helped figure out the last mile problem and popularized parcel delivery, and how scientific management theories influenced everything the company did. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Naomi Kresge, Ashleigh Furlong, Sonja Wind and Fabienne Kinzelmann

item.title: How an American AI Company Uses Chinese Open-Weight Models
item.description:
This week, we got news that the Trump administration is reportedly considering a requirement for US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models. Any effort to discourage US businesses from using Chinese open-source could be a big deal for both the AI industry and the market, where investors are still debating whether customers will ultimately be willing to pay for pricier homegrown frontier models versus cheaper alternatives. Everyone remembers last year's 'DeepSeek moment' for AI, when a Chinese company released a cheaper model that seemed nearly as good as cutting-edge US ones. So why do businesses actually use open-source? In this episode, we talk to Daniel Saedi, co-founder of Minerva, to better understand how an AI native company chooses its models. He breaks down how exactly his company mixes and matches models for specific use cases, the risk of obliterated models, and the issue of data sovereignty. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: This Is The Problem With AI's Most Bullish Chart
item.description:
It has been a historic week for AI: The Anthropic IPO and the ongoing situation at Nvidia headline a head-spinning time for the industry. Despite Nvidia's earnings outlook looking good, and despite the scale of the Anthropic IPO there are so many open questions about the state of the industry right now. On today's two-part episode, first we speak with Stanley Lee, the chief product officer at Liquid Compute, and he explains why Wall Street and Silicon Valley seem to be talking past each other, and what fragilities are emerging in the credit market for GPUs. All those charts that show rising GPU rental rates, Lee tells us, might not be as industry-bullish as they first appear. Then, we turn to Paul Kedrosky, a managing partner at SK Ventures, and we discuss why “number goes up and to the right” does not necessarily prove the viability of the capex involved in the AI buildout and if Nvidia will remain the central bank for AI. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: The Impossible Trilemma Hanging Over the Nvidia Crisis
item.description:
Tian Yang, CIO and manager of the VPX fund at Variant Perception, recently published a report called “The Sovereign Impossible Trinity” that is especially salient right now. Yang's thesis is that the US-China rivalry is exposing three main policy trade-offs: The necessity of sovereignty (which both of the great powers insist on) means that neither state can assure they can maintain the trio of guns (or the AI 'arms race'), butter (social spending), and sound money because of physical constraints, political conditions, and inflation. Given that the US-China AI arms race forms the backdrop of the upheaval at Nvidia, you can't understand Jensen Huang's resignation without considering geopolitical and global economic conditions. Yang talks to us today about why Jensen might be our era's Oppenheimer and what it means that the biggest powers in the world can't maintain sound monetary policy while also upholding defense and entitlements. (Source: Bloomberg)

And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. President Donald Trump is beginning a week-long trip to Asia focused on trade, with stops in the Philippines, China and a historic trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Pressure is mounting on Nvidia days after it ousted Jensen Huang as chief executive officer, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urging the company to make a “dramatic” leadership shakeup. The Financial Times reported that Huang has been discussing the idea of returning to the company he co-founded more than three decades ago. Today's guest: Charu Chanana, Saxo, Chief Investment Strategist. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Why a $2 Billion Law Firm Suddenly Collapsed
item.description:
At the end of October, seemingly overnight, a major law firm called Weil Gotshal announced it was winding down after a number of partners departed and talks of a merger with another firm failed. So how did a $2 billion big law firm collapse in the span of a few weeks? In 2015, Yale Law professor John Morley published a paper called "Why Law Firms Collapse," that now looks very prescient, with his idea of a “partner run," or the law firm version of a bank run. What is especially interesting about Morley's paper is his forensic examination of partner-led businesses and the idea that the model might be inherently fragile. In this episode, we talk to Morley about his newly relevant paper, the collapse of Weil Gotshal, whether AI will really change how law firms are run, and the future of big law. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: The Perfect Storm That Clobbered Hedge Funds
item.description:
Even before the midterms, the AI trade was weakening. Just look at all the headlines from October in the hedge fund world — it was one of the bloodiest periods the industry has faced in recent memory. Now, after the blue wave, things continue to look uncertain. So what's going to happen with the AI buildout now? And what about the big Anthropic IPO? Today's episode is a two-parter, one that examines both the hedge fund carnage of the last few weeks and the broader macro conditions we find ourselves in after the midterm elections. We speak with two of our Bloomberg News colleagues — Nishant Kumar, chief correspondent for hedge funds, and macro strategist Michael Ball — and they help lay out why October was a historic month for hedge funds and what they are paying attention to now as jitters from the AI trade continue to work their way through the market. (Source: Bloomberg)

What he means is that it's the last free and unlimited city service — there is no opt-in; it is not means tested. Goodman — who is the DSNY's deputy commissioner for public affairs and customer experience — tells us that the city deals with 24 million pounds of trash every day, and on today's podcast, he explains the logistical dance required to sort through all that garbage. We also get into why NYC produces less trash than you might think, the DSNY's new containerization program (and the new side-loading trucks they built in less than 18 months), and why recycling is not a scam. item.title: How the Iran War Is Making Alaskans Both Richer and Poorer

This means higher costs for households in most states, but in Alaska, the state government is bringing in new revenue from its high oil production to offset those higher costs.
